findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct or drop the `reducer/marker.py:33` citation as a 'guards correctly' example — line 33 is a bare unguarded `fcntl.flock` (its `except OSError` will not catch the None `AttributeError`); either cite a genuinely-guarded sibling or note marker.py carries the same latent bug and state whether it is in scope.
evidence: Plan quote: 'Sibling modules already guard correctly (`_snapshot/git_fetch.py:79`, `_snapshot/janitor.py:430`, `reducer/marker.py:33`), which makes `lock.py` an outlier rather than a deliberate choice.'
git_fetch.py:79 = `if fcntl is not None:` (verified guarded)
janitor.py:430 = `if fcntl is not None:` (verified guarded)
reducer/marker.py:33 = `fcntl.flock(lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX)` inside `try: ... except OSError:` with NO `is not None` check; import guard at lines 8-11 sets `fcntl = None`
AttributeError from `None.flock` is not an OSError, so marker.py's except clause would not catch it
findings.finding: The plan cites `reducer/marker.py:33` as a sibling module that 'already guards correctly' against absent fcntl, but Read shows line 33 is a bare `fcntl.flock(lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX)` (and line 38 `fcntl.flock(..., LOCK_UN)`) with no `if fcntl is not None` guard at the use site — only the import try/except (lines 8-11) and an `except OSError` (line 39). When `fcntl is None` on Windows, `None.flock` raises `AttributeError`, which is NOT an `OSError` and would propagate uncaught. marker.py is therefore NOT correctly guarded, contrary to the plan's assertion.
findings.location: Class section: 'Sibling modules already guard correctly (... reducer/marker.py:33 ...)'
scenarios: A reader relies on the 'outlier' framing to conclude marker.py is a safe model to copy, when marker.py in fact shares the same latent Windows AttributeError bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the marker.py citation with a module that actually gates the use site (git_fetch.py:79 and janitor.py:430 already do), or explicitly acknowledge marker.py shares the unguarded-fcntl defect and clarify whether S1 covers it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a real cross-process contention probe on windows-latest: process A takes the exclusive leg then is killed (or holds), process B must be able to reclaim only after A's handle closes and must NEVER reclaim while A is live — proving the dies-with-process release semantics of the chosen primitive.
evidence: AC2: 'the Windows proof (kernel-mediated file lock released on handle close, hence on process death) written out in the docstring'
Testing step 2: 'Platform-seam simulation on this POSIX host ... a Windows-shaped primitive supplied, so the Windows branch of the real acquire() runs here rather than being asserted about'
A stubbed primitive on POSIX cannot exhibit real msvcrt/LockFileEx handle-close release semantics — the very property the staleness proof depends on
findings.finding: The load-bearing Windows invariant — that the chosen exclusive primitive (msvcrt.locking / LockFileEx) is released on handle close and therefore dies with the holding process, exactly as flock does — is ASSERTED in AC2's docstring requirement but never empirically validated. The Testing section validates the Windows branch only via a stubbed primitive on a POSIX host (step 2), and AC5 only counts flock AttributeErrors == 0. No probe demonstrates the actual dies-with-process release semantics of the selected Windows primitive.
scenarios: The chosen Windows primitive does NOT release on abnormal process termination (e.g. a userspace or mutex-style substitute is selected), silently reintroducing the exact reclaim-a-live-holder corruption the story exists to prevent
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC and Windows-only test that spawns a second process holding the exclusive leg on the same tracker's .ticket-write.lock, asserts acquire() from a competing process fails while the holder is alive, and (kill the holder) succeeds afterward — run on windows-latest.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an acceptance criterion that runs a concurrency/contention suite on windows-latest exercising the real exclusive leg (not the POSIX-only or stubbed path), so the exclusivity guarantee is proven on the platform that changed.
evidence: AC4 verifies via tests/integration/test_concurrency_regression.py etc. described as 'the existing concurrency gates' / 'POSIX behaviour is unchanged'
AC5 only checks 'flock AttributeError count ... is 0'
No AC drives concurrent writers on windows-latest to prove the exclusive leg actually serializes writes and blocks live-holder reclamation
findings.finding: The core end-state claim — 'a Windows run reaches the same exclusivity guarantee' with fcntl_held=True remaining true — has no proving command that exercises live cross-process contention on Windows. AC4's concurrency regression suites are explicitly the 'unchanged POSIX run' only; AC1/AC2 run against a stubbed-absent fcntl on POSIX; AC5 only greps the AttributeError count. Thus the reclamation-race safety the story is fundamentally about is never exercised on the platform whose behavior changed.
scenarios: Windows leg compiles and stops the AttributeError (AC5 green) but does not actually provide mutual exclusion under concurrency, so store writes race on Windows undetected

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a live cross-process acceptance criterion on windows-latest that proves the chosen exclusive primitive both blocks a second concurrent acquire() and releases on the first holder's death (the reclamation-safety property), not merely that the flock AttributeError count is 0.
evidence: 'the exclusive-leg selector is driven with the fcntl primitive stubbed absent and a Windows-shaped primitive supplied, so the Windows branch of the real acquire() runs here rather than being asserted about'
AC4 names tests/integration/test_concurrency_regression.py, test_store_concurrency.py, test_reads_under_sync_contention.py — all POSIX no-regression, none Windows
The plan itself states 'A userspace substitute that does not die with its holder does NOT satisfy the precondition' — precisely the property a stubbed primitive cannot demonstrate
findings.finding: The load-bearing property of the new Windows exclusive leg — that the kernel lock is released on process death, making reclamation race-safe (the fcntl_held=True precondition) — is validated only by a docstring argument and a single-process POSIX seam simulation with a 'Windows-shaped primitive supplied', plus a flock-AttributeError count of 0 on Windows. No acceptance criterion drives TWO real concurrent processes on windows-latest to prove the chosen primitive (msvcrt.locking / LockFileEx) actually blocks a second holder AND releases on the first holder's death. The concurrency regression suites in AC4 run only the existing POSIX proof.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC: on windows-latest, spawn two rebar processes contending on the same tracker's .ticket-write.lock; assert the second blocks/fails while the first holds, and that killing the first process lets the second acquire — proving the leg is kernel-mediated and dies-with-process.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Select ONE Windows exclusive primitive (not an 'or') and route the die-with-process release-semantics question through a SPIKE that verifies, against MS docs and a real killed-process cross-process test on windows-latest, that the lock is dropped before a second acquirer can reclaim — before committing the full fix.
evidence: Plan: 'msvcrt.locking(fd, LK_NBLCK, …) or LockFileEx via ctypes/pywin32 — that provides the same kernel-mediated, dies-with-the-process exclusivity flock provides'
AC2 requires proof that the lock is 'released on handle close, hence on process death' — asserted, not demonstrated
EVIDENCE CLASS: Unverified — msvcrt resolves UNRESOLVED on the POSIX review host (Windows-only stdlib); LockFileEx/pywin32 cannot be probed here
MS-documented risk (surfaced in prior review cache): LockFileEx release-on-termination is asynchronous, a possible violation of the mkdir reclamation precondition
findings.finding: The Windows exclusive leg is left as an unresolved 'or' between msvcrt.locking and LockFileEx (ctypes/pywin32), whose die-with-process release semantics differ and are UNVERIFIED. Microsoft documents that lock release on abnormal process termination for LockFileEx is asynchronous ('depends upon available system resources'), which can leave a lock briefly held after the owner dies — directly threatening the load-bearing fcntl_held=True reclamation precondition the whole story rests on. This capability equivalence is asserted, not verified, and is the crux of the plan.
findings.location: Section 'What a correct fix requires' item 1 / AC line 2
scenarios: Windows process holding the exclusive leg is killed; a second acquirer reclaims the mkdir lock during the async release window while state is still live
Chosen primitive is process-scoped (msvcrt byte-range) rather than handle/kernel-lifetime, silently breaking fcntl_held=True
findings.suggested_fix: Add a SPIKE step that (a) picks LockFileEx-on-handle vs msvcrt.locking with a stated rationale, (b) checks MS documentation on lock release timing at abnormal termination, and (c) runs a windows-latest test where process A takes the leg and is killed and process B must be unable to reclaim until A is truly gone; only then commit to fcntl_held=True on Windows, else narrow reclamation per AC2's alternative.

findings.checklist_item: Specify how the Windows leg's v2 ownership stamp flows through the shared _stamp_is_stale decision table (lock_owner.py rows 4-6): what host/ns values the Windows stamp writes, whether the same-host pid-probe leg (_pid_alive via os.kill) is valid on Windows, and which row licenses reclamation — so the reworked proof is complete rather than only asserted in the docstring.
evidence: Plan: 'The Windows leg's proof must be stated explicitly in the docstring and must be its own argument, not a copy of the POSIX one.'
lock_owner.py:428-433 routes on stamped_ns != _read_pid_namespace_id(); rows 5-6 depend on pid namespaces that do not exist on Windows
lock_owner.py:288-299 _pid_alive uses os.kill(pid, 0); its Windows semantics differ from POSIX and are not addressed
_acquire_mkdir (lock.py:362,370) calls _mkdir_lock_is_stale(..., fcntl_held=True) which delegates into this shared table
findings.finding: The plan mandates a Windows-specific staleness proof in _acquire_mkdir's docstring but does not specify how the Windows leg's v2 ownership stamp participates in the SHARED decision table (_stamp_is_stale rows 4-6 in lock_owner.py), which is POSIX-shaped: it keys on pid namespaces (_read_pid_namespace_id, absent on Windows) and _pid_alive (os.kill(pid,0), whose Windows behaviour differs). Without stating what ns/host the Windows stamp writes and whether the same-host pid-probe leg (row 5) is valid on Windows, the reworked proof is incomplete and the fcntl_held=True (or its narrowed replacement) may route through a branch that never applies or misjudges liveness on Windows.
findings.location: 'What a correct fix requires' item 2 (reworked staleness proof) and AC2
scenarios: A Windows writer dies holding .ticket-write.lock.d; a second Windows acquirer must reclaim via _stamp_is_stale but the same-host branch depends on _pid_alive/_read_pid_namespace_id semantics the plan never pins down
The Windows v2 stamp's ns field is unset/unknown, silently routing reclamation through the foreign-namespace branch (row 6) or the ceiling instead of the intended fcntl proof

findings.checklist_item: Resolve whether LockFileEx/msvcrt asynchronous lock-release-on-termination ('depends upon available system resources' per MS docs) can violate the reclamation invariant, and state the mitigation (or narrow the Windows reclamation path) rather than assert immediate release.
evidence: Plan text (AC2): 'the Windows proof (kernel-mediated file lock released on handle close, hence on process death) written out in the docstring'

Retrieved: Microsoft LockFileEx docs (learn.microsoft.com/.../nf-fileapi-lockfileex) — 'If a process terminates with a portion of a file locked or closes a file that has outstanding locks, the locks are unlocked by the operating system. However, the time it takes for the operating system to unlock these locks depends upon available system resources.'

This async-release window is the exact kind of gap the POSIX flock proof relied on being closed (kernel-mediated, immediate on inode); the plan carries the invariant forward but does not resolve whether the Windows release lag can leave a live-holder's lock apparently free during reclamation.
findings.finding: The plan's Windows staleness proof asserts the lock is 'released on handle close, hence on process death' as though release is synchronous/immediate, but the LockFileEx capability actually releases asynchronously.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria bullet 2 / 'What a correct fix requires' item 2
scenarios: A Windows process holding the write lock is killed; the OS has not yet released the lock, or conversely releases it with a delay long enough that a reclaiming process observing 'no lock' proceeds while cleanup is still in flight.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Windows-leg docstring proof, address the documented async-release window explicitly: either argue why acquire()'s exclusive-acquire attempt (which will still fail while the OS holds the lock) closes the window, or — if it cannot be proven — do not pass fcntl_held=True on Windows and narrow reclamation as the plan's own item 2 fallback allows.

evidence: 'with NO exclusive leg available, acquire() raises and never creates .ticket-write.lock.d'

'If the Windows leg cannot support fcntl_held=True, the reclamation path must be narrowed on Windows rather than the flag falsified' — a disposition-affecting narrowing with no stated caller-facing disposition
findings.finding: The plan adds a new failure arm — when NO exclusive leg is available, acquire() raises and never creates .ticket-write.lock.d (AC3) — but never states that arm's disposition. It does not say, with an explicit disposition word, whether a Windows host lacking any exclusive-lock primitive surfaces a FATAL/permanent 'unsupported platform' error or something a caller might treat as retryable/transient.

findings.checklist_item: Consider and explicitly rule in/out established cross-platform file-locking prior art (filelock/portalocker) before hand-rolling the Windows leg, and justify the chosen approach against it (including whether it satisfies the dies-with-process precondition).
evidence: Plan text: 'A real alternative exclusive leg on Windows — msvcrt.locking(fd, LK_NBLCK, …) or LockFileEx via ctypes/pywin32'

Retrieved (runebook.dev msvcrt.LK_NBLCK page): 'For reliable and cross-platform file locking, you should avoid msvcrt entirely. The filelock library is highly recommended for robust, cross-platform file locking in Python.'

Retrieved (StackOverflow, 'Opening a file on Windows with exclusive locking'): 'There still doesn't appear to be a way to generate an exclusive lock with Python's standard library' — corroborating that raw msvcrt exclusivity is fraught.
The plan gives no rationale for preferring a bespoke primitive over these libraries, nor whether they satisfy the dies-with-process precondition.
findings.finding: The plan hand-rolls a Windows exclusive-lock leg via msvcrt/ctypes/pywin32 without considering established cross-platform file-locking prior art (filelock / portalocker).
scenarios: Implementation reinvents locking semantics that filelock/portalocker already encapsulate and test across platforms, re-incurring known msvcrt sharing-mode/exclusivity pitfalls the plan does not enumerate.
